name: Bilal Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work nights at a big grocery warehouse out on the ring road, ten at night till six in the morning. I pick orders for supermarkets, mostly the chilled section, so milk, yoghurt and packs of chicken stacked onto roll cages. A voice in my headset tells me the aisle and the slot, I read the check number back, I lift, I move on. By about three in the morning my back is talking louder than the headset.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the lads on my shift, and I like that when the shift ends it's done, nobody rings me at home. What wears me out is the rate. They want 160 cases an hour, and on a heavy night I'm at 140 and the team leader comes round with his tablet. I've been there just under two years and I'm still not as quick as the old hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, leave us alone then. At work we'd joke that the robots were all talk, same as the self-checkouts that keep breaking. Online I don't post much, maybe I'd share something from the union page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my problem was never AI. My problem is the pick rate, the night shifts and the rent going up every year. Lena, my girlfriend, and I put over a third of what we earn into the flat, and that doesn't get better because the robots stayed in the lab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, really. I'd keep my head down, keep paying the union dues, and try to put an extra hundred a month aside on top of what we already save. We've got about three months of bills put by, and I'd like it to be four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kind of relieved, but tired. It's like being told the storm isn't coming when you're already wet from the rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the rate. What happens if you don't hit it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First you get a chat, then a written note, then you're on a plan. A guy called Marek on my shift got walked out last spring after three notes. I haven't had a note yet, but I count the cases in my head every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Lena say about your nights?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She works days in a care home, so we pass each other like ships. Sunday is the only night we both sleep at the same time. She says I should get my forklift licence and get onto days, and she's probably right, I just keep putting it off.

say: I'd tell the lads the **robot talk** was hype, like the self-checkouts that keep breaking.
I'd share a **union post** online rather than write anything myself.
think: My real worries are the **pick rate**, the night shifts and rising rent, not AI.
A plateau leaves the **flat costs** eating over a third of what Lena and I earn.
do: Keep picking chilled orders on nights and keep **paying union dues**.
Add an **extra hundred** a month to savings to stretch three months of bills to four.
feel: **Relieved** that nothing big is coming, but worn down by the nights.
Still **uneasy**, because the rate target hangs over every shift.
S0.quote: My problem was never AI. My problem is the pick rate, the night shifts and the rent going up every year.
fieldNote: Even with AI going nowhere, the **pick rate** is the threat he names first.
A colleague, Marek, was **walked out** after three notes; that story shapes how he sees the job.
He knows the **forklift licence** would help and admits he keeps putting it off.

steps.text: Keep picking chilled orders on the night shift at the ring road depot
Go to union branch meetings and keep paying dues
Add an extra hundred a month to the savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: if they bring in machines, the workers should get a cut of what it saves. I'd say it in the canteen and I'd say it at the union meeting. I'm not against progress, I'm against it all going to the shareholders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking stuff would go first, the people in the office who plan the waves and order the stock. My bit is lifting cases, so I'd have a few years. But I know our company has been looking at those shuttle systems for the frozen store, and once that works there's no reason it stops at frozen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get something in writing, like no compulsory redundancies without retraining. I'd stop eating out on Fridays and put that money aside. If they offered a course on the new kit I'd probably go, though I'd hate every minute of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground is moving very slowly under my feet. Not a fall, more like a slope I keep sliding down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, Gloria in the transport office. She books the lorries and sorts the paperwork, and that's exactly the kind of job the software eats. She's worked there fifteen years and she's the one who always remembers your birthday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hate a course. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I left school at sixteen. Every time someone puts a screen in front of me I feel stupid, and the new kit is all screens. They changed the headset menus last year and it took me two weeks to stop pressing the wrong button. I know that's on me, but that's how it is.

say: I'd argue in the canteen that workers need a **fair share** of what machines save.
I'd raise **retraining guarantees** at the union meeting, not just complain about the bosses.
think: The **office jobs** like wave planning and ordering would go before my lifting job.
Once the **shuttle system** works in frozen, the company won't stop there.
do: Push the union for a **written promise** of retraining before any redundancies.
Stop the **Friday meals out** and save that money instead.
Sign up for a **course** on the new kit if one is offered.
feel: Like **sliding slowly** down a slope rather than falling.
**Embarrassed** at how hard he finds new screens and menus.
S1.quote: Every time someone puts a screen in front of me I feel stupid, and the new kit is all screens.
fieldNote: He is **pro-union** and frames the change as a question of who gets the savings.
He worries for **office colleagues** first, which shows he understands thinking work goes earlier.
His **fear of screens** is the real barrier, and he says so openly.

steps.text: Ask the union rep for written retraining guarantees
Drop Friday meals out and save the money
Take the company course on the new frozen-store kit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when nobody is in charge. I'd be posting for the first time in my life, probably about taxing the companies that use robots. At work I'd be telling everyone to join the union now, not when the letters come out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For two years nothing would change on the floor, but the office would empty out. Then a robot that picks a pack of chicken as fast as me turns up around 2031, and every warehouse round here buys the same one. I'd be thirty-one with no qualifications, and I'm out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd stop any big spending and try to build the savings to six months. I'd finally do the forklift licence, even if it only buys me a year or two. I'd go to every union meeting and help get people signed up, because a strong union is the only thing that gets you a decent payout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, to be honest. Like waiting for a letter you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her that her job is safer than mine, because people in a care home still want a person holding their hand. Then I'd probably ask if she'd mind carrying us for a while. I hate saying that out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car. We've got an old hatchback we only use on weekends, and the insurance alone is a month of savings. After that the phone contracts, then the holiday we keep talking about and never take.

say: I'd post about **taxing companies** that replace workers with robots.
I'd tell everyone on shift to **join the union** before the redundancy letters arrive.
think: The **office** empties first, then around 2031 a robot takes over **picking**.
At thirty-one with **no qualifications**, every local warehouse would want the same robot.
do: Freeze big spending and push savings from three to **six months**.
Get the **forklift licence** now, even if it only buys a year or two.
Help **sign people up** to the union to win better payouts.
feel: **Sick**, like waiting for a letter he knows is coming.
S2.quote: A robot that picks a pack of chicken as fast as me turns up around 2031, and every warehouse round here buys the same one.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year gap** clearly: the office goes first, his picking later.
He would lean on his girlfriend's **care job**, and admitting it pains him.
The **old car** is the first cut, a sign he is thinking practically despite the fear.

steps.text: Sell the weekend hatchback to save the insurance money
Book the forklift licence course this year
Recruit night-shift colleagues into the union
Lean on Lena's care home wage if picking goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, but louder: tax the robots and use the money for people. With five years' warning there's no excuse for the government to be caught out. I'd say it at work and I'd sign every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years before the thinking AI, then eight before the robots reach my aisle. That's long enough that I'd probably waste the first three years telling myself it won't happen to me. I know myself, I'm slow to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the forklift licence in the first year, because at least it gets me onto days. I'd keep saving and I'd vote for whoever promises a proper plan for people like me. And I'd ask the union to fight for a retraining fund paid for by the company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not in a panic. It's like knowing you'll have to move house in a few years and not wanting to pack yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd waste the first three years. What would stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone sitting me down. If I have to find a course myself on a website, I won't. Someone has to say it starts Monday and it's paid. Lena would have to nag me, and she would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you retrain into, if you had to choose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I really don't know, that's the honest answer. Maybe something with people, like Lena does, because a robot holding someone's hand sounds wrong. But I'm not sure I'm the caring type.

say: I'd say five years of warning means the **government** has no excuse to be caught out.
I'd sign petitions to **tax robots** and spend the money on workers.
think: With **eight years** before robots reach picking, I'd likely waste the first three.
I'm **slow to move** unless someone puts a paid course in front of me.
do: Get the **forklift licence** in the first year and move onto day shifts.
Vote for whoever offers a **real plan** for warehouse workers.
Ask the union to fight for a **company-paid** retraining fund.
feel: **Worried** but not panicking, like dreading a house move.
S3.quote: If I have to find a course myself on a website, I won't. Someone has to say it starts Monday and it's paid.
fieldNote: He is **honest about inertia** and expects to delay without a push.
He has **no clear second career** in mind and admits it.
**Politics** and the union are his main levers, more than personal change.

steps.text: Pass the forklift licence and ask for day shifts
Vote for candidates promising a robot tax
Press the union for a company-paid retraining fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so let's use it properly. The company and the government should start the training now, not in year nine. I'd probably say it in a union meeting and then forget about it for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirteen years before robots are picking, I'd be forty. Part of me thinks that's someone else's problem. The other part knows better. At forty with no trade and a bad back, starting again is a rough place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much in the first year, if I'm honest. Keep saving, keep the union going, maybe start the forklift licence. I'd want to see the robots actually working somewhere before I changed my whole life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. It's far off enough that I can sleep, but it's there in the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you act sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it with my own eyes. If a mate at another depot told me their robots were picking chilled faster than people, I'd move. Until then, it's just talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change any plans with Lena?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about kids one day. With ten years' warning, maybe I'd want them sooner, while I still have a steady wage. That's a strange thing for a robot to decide, isn't it?

say: I'd say a decade is **plenty of time** if training starts now, not in year nine.
I'd raise it at **one union meeting**, then probably let it drop for a while.
think: At **forty** with a bad back and no trade, starting again would be rough.
Part of me calls it **someone else's problem**, and I know that isn't true.
do: Keep **saving** and stay active in the union.
Start the **forklift licence** but wait to see robots working before any big change.
feel: **Calmer**, able to sleep, with the worry sitting at the back of his mind.
S4.quote: At forty with no trade and a bad back, starting again is a rough place to be.
fieldNote: The **long runway** lets him relax, perhaps too much.
He would act only on **seeing robots** working at another depot.
AI timing even shapes **family plans**: he might want children sooner.

steps.text: Keep the monthly transfer into the savings account going
Wait until a nearby depot runs picking robots before changing jobs
Talk with Lena about having children sooner

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years is nothing, I'd still be finding the courage to sign up for a course. What would help is a company that has to pay for retraining before it buys a robot, and a union strong enough to make it stick.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the body. Picking breaks people, my back at twenty-seven is proof. If a robot did the lifting and I still had a wage, I'd be the first one cheering. It's never the robot I'm scared of, it's who owns it.

headlineQuote: If a robot did the lifting and I still had a wage, I'd be the first one cheering. It's never the robot I'm scared of, it's who owns it.
portrait: Bilal is a **27-year-old night picker** in a chilled grocery warehouse, still below the pick rate after two years.
He is **pro-union** and blames owners and shareholders, not machines, for what change might do.
He is **slow with screens** and admits he only moves when someone puts a paid course in front of him.
His mood runs from **uneasy** in a plateau to **alarmed** when robots could reach picking by 2031.
He would lean on his girlfriend Lena's **care home wage** and cut the car first.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short for someone as slow to start as him.
whatWouldHelp: Companies made to **fund retraining** before buying robots, backed by a strong union.
